front: A single truck needs a CDL at what weight rating?
back: 26,001 pounds or more GVWR
why: Remember: 26,001 is the magic CDL number.

front: How many people can a vehicle carry before it needs a CDL?
back: 16 or more, counting the driver

front: What is a Class A vehicle?
back: A combination over 26,000 lbs, towing over 10,000 lbs
why: A is for the big rigs, like a tractor and trailer.

front: What BAC is illegal when driving a CMV?
back: 0.04% or more
why: Half the car limit of 0.08%.

front: First DUI in a CMV: how long do you lose your CDL?
back: At least 1 year

front: First DUI while hauling placarded hazmat: CDL loss?
back: At least 3 years

front: What happens for a second DUI-type offense?
back: You lose your CDL for life

front: Refusing an alcohol test: what is the penalty?
back: Lose CDL at least 1 year (first time)
why: Driving a CMV means you agree to be tested.

front: Any alcohol under 0.04% in your body: penalty?
back: Out of service for 24 hours

front: Name 3 serious traffic violations.
back: Speeding 15+ over, tailgating, reckless driving
why: Bad lane changes also count.

front: 2 serious violations in 3 years: CDL loss?
back: At least 60 days

front: 3 serious violations in 3 years: CDL loss?
back: At least 120 days

front: First time breaking an out-of-service order: penalty?
back: SD: lose CDL 180 days
why: National chapter says at least 90 days. SD law says 180.

front: Lose your car license for DUI. What about your CDL?
back: You lose your CDL for 1 year
why: Car tickets can cost you your CDL.

front: How soon must you tell your boss about a traffic ticket?
back: Within 30 days
why: Any ticket except parking, in any vehicle.

front: License suspended: how soon must you tell your boss?
back: Within 2 business days

front: What is the most important reason to inspect?
back: Safety

front: Minimum tread depth on front tires?
back: 4/32 inch
why: Front tires steer, so they need more tread.

front: Minimum tread depth on all other tires?
back: 2/32 inch

front: How much steering wheel play is too much?
back: More than 10 degrees (about 2 inches)
why: Measured on a 20-inch wheel.

front: How many missing leaf-spring leaves put you out of service?
back: One-fourth (1/4) or more

front: What 3 kinds of emergency gear must you carry?
back: Fire extinguisher, spare fuses, warning devices
why: Fuses not needed if you have circuit breakers.

front: How many reflective warning triangles must you carry?
What should the ABS light do after you start the engine?
back: Come on, then go off
why: If it stays on, the ABS is not working.

front: How do you check hydraulic brakes for leaks?
back: Pump 3 times, press and hold 5 seconds
why: If the pedal moves, there may be a leak.

front: When must you first check cargo securement on a trip?
back: Within the first 50 miles

front: After that, how often must you check cargo?
back: Every 150 miles or 3 hours
why: Whichever comes first.

front: Which way should you back and turn?
back: Toward the driver's side
why: You can see better out your own window.

front: Most important hand signal to agree on with a helper?
back: Stop

front: When should you downshift for a hill?
back: Before you start down the hill
why: Use a gear lower than you'd use to climb it.

front: When should you turn the retarder off?
back: On wet, icy, or snowy roads
why: It can make the drive wheels skid.

front: How far ahead should you look?
back: 12 to 15 seconds

front: At highway speed, 12-15 seconds ahead is how far?
back: About 1/4 mile
why: In town, it is about 1 block.

front: Objects in a convex mirror look how?
back: Smaller and farther away than they are

front: How do you warn drivers behind that you will slow?
back: Tap the brakes to flash brake lights

front: Stopped on the shoulder. How soon must warning devices go out?
back: Within 10 minutes

front: Divided highway stop: where do the 3 triangles go?
back: 10, 100, and 200 feet behind you
why: All toward the oncoming traffic.

front: Two-way road stop: where do the triangles go?
back: 10 ft behind, 100 ft behind, 100 ft ahead

front: What makes up total stopping distance?
back: Perception + reaction + braking distance

front: Total stopping distance at 55 mph on dry road?
back: About 419 feet
why: More than a football field at 60 mph.

front: Double your speed. What happens to braking distance?
back: It becomes 4 times longer

front: Do empty trucks stop faster than loaded ones?
back: No. Empty trucks need more room to stop
why: An empty truck has less traction.

front: On a wet road, slow down by how much?
back: About 1/3 (55 down to 35 mph)

front: On packed snow, slow down by how much?
back: By 1/2 or more

front: What freezes first, bridges or roads?
back: Bridges
why: Watch out near 32°F.

front: What is black ice?
back: Thin clear ice that makes the road look wet

front: When is a wet road most slippery?
back: Just after rain starts
why: Rain mixes with oil on the road.

front: Hydroplaning can start at what speed?
back: As low as 30 mph

front: You are hydroplaning. What do you do?
back: Let off the gas and push in the clutch
why: Do not use the brakes.

front: When should you slow down for a curve?
back: Before you enter it
why: Braking in a curve can lock the wheels.

front: You should always be able to stop within what distance?
back: The distance you can see ahead

front: Number 1 cause of injury and death in work zones?
back: Speeding traffic

front: Which space around your truck matters most?
back: The space ahead

front: Following distance rule under 40 mph?
back: 1 second per 10 feet of vehicle length

front: Over 40 mph, how much time do you add?
back: 1 more second

front: 40-foot truck under 40 mph: following distance?
back: 4 seconds

front: 40-foot truck over 40 mph: following distance?
back: 5 seconds

front: Someone is tailgating you. What should you do?
back: Add space ahead and slow down gently
why: Do not speed up or flash your brake lights.

front: Are posted bridge heights always correct?
back: No
why: New paving or packed snow can lower clearance.

front: Empty or loaded: which van sits higher?
back: Empty

front: Right turn: how do you stop cars passing on your right?
back: Keep the back near the curb; swing wide late

front: Should you swing left before a right turn?
back: No
why: A car may try to pass you on the right.

front: Left turn: when do you start turning?
back: After you reach the center of the intersection

front: Two left-turn lanes: which one do you use?
back: The right-hand turn lane

front: Emergency vehicle stopped on the shoulder. What should you do?
back: Slow down and move over a lane if safe

front: Name the 2 main types of distraction.
back: Physical and mental
why: Texting is both, so it is the worst.

front: What phone can you use while driving a CMV?
back: Hands-free only, placed close to you

front: An aggressive driver comes at you. What first?
back: Get out of their way

front: Should you wear tinted glasses at night?
back: No
why: They cut the light you need to see.

front: Name signs that you are too tired to drive.
back: Yawning, heavy eyes, drifting, missing exits

front: On long trips, how often should you take a break?
back: About every 100 miles or 2 hours

front: What is the only real cure for being sleepy?
back: Sleep
why: Coffee and drugs do not fix fatigue.

front: How far ahead do low beams let you see?
back: About 250 feet

front: How far ahead do high beams let you see?
back: About 350 to 500 feet

front: Dim your high beams within what distance of a car?
back: 500 feet
why: Oncoming or one you follow.

front: Best advice for driving in fog?
back: Don't. Pull off until it clears.

front: If you must drive in fog, which lights do you use?
back: Low beams, fog lights, and 4-way flashers

front: No spray coming off other cars' tires means what?
back: Ice has formed on the road

front: Must drive through deep water. How?
back: Low gear, light brake pressure, then dry brakes
why: Light braking keeps water and mud out.

front: In hot weather, how often should you check tires?
back: Every 2 hours or 100 miles

front: Tire pressure is high on a hot day. Let air out?
back: No
why: It will be too low when the tire cools.

front: When is it safe to remove the radiator cap?
back: Only after the system has cooled
why: Hot steam and water can spray out.

front: What is bleeding tar?
back: Tar rising up on hot roads; very slippery

front: Which vehicles must always stop at rail crossings?
back: Buses with passengers and hazmat vehicles

front: No stop line: how close to the rail do you stop?
back: 15 to 50 feet from the nearest rail

front: Can you count on hearing a train horn?
back: No
why: Some crossings ban horns, and cabs are noisy.

front: One train passes on a double track. What next?
back: Check for a second train before crossing

front: How long does a tractor-trailer take to clear 1 track?
back: At least 14 seconds

front: How long to clear a double track?
back: More than 15 seconds

front: Can you shift gears while crossing tracks?
back: No

front: Name trailers that can get stuck on raised crossings.
back: Lowboys, car carriers, moving vans
why: Low-slung trailers hang up on the tracks.

front: Stuck on the tracks. What first?
back: Get out and away from the tracks
why: Then call the number posted at the crossing or 911.

front: What is brake fade?
back: Hot brakes lose power
why: You must press harder and harder to slow down.

front: When should you pick a low gear for a downgrade?
back: Before you start down
why: Once speed builds, you may not get into gear.

front: On a downgrade, brakes are used with what?
back: Engine braking; brakes are only extra help

front: Downhill braking: when do you release the brakes?
back: About 5 mph below your safe speed

front: Safe speed is 40 mph. Brake down to what?
back: 35 mph, then let go
why: Each brake use lasts about 3 seconds.

front: Turning or stopping: which is usually faster to miss something?
back: Turning

front: Should you brake while making a quick turn?
back: No
why: The wheels can lock and you skid.

front: What is counter-steering?
back: Turning back the other way after you clear it

front: Car drifts into your lane head-on. Which way do you steer?
back: To the right

front: Leaving the road: when can you start braking?
back: When you slow to about 20 mph
why: Then brake very gently.

front: What is controlled braking?
back: Brake hard without locking the wheels

front: What is stab braking?
back: Brake fully, let up when wheels lock, repeat

front: Brake pedal goes to the floor. What do you do?
back: Downshift, pump brakes, use parking brake

front: Brakes fail going downhill. What is your best hope?
back: An escape ramp

front: A tire blows. What do you do first?
back: Hold the wheel firmly; stay off the brake

front: What does ABS do?
back: Keeps wheels from locking in hard braking

front: How do you brake with ABS?
back: The same way as always

front: Name the 4 causes of skids.
back: Over-braking, over-steering, too much gas, too fast
why: Most bad skids come from driving too fast.

front: A drive-wheel skid in a rig can cause what?
back: A jackknife

front: How do you fix a drive-wheel braking skid?
back: Stop braking, then counter-steer

front: How do you stop a front-wheel skid?
back: Let the truck slow down
why: Stop turning and braking so hard.

front: What are the 3 steps at a crash scene?
back: Protect the area, call for help, aid the hurt

front: At a crash, what do you do first?
back: Protect the area from another crash

front: When should you move a badly hurt person?
back: Only if fire or traffic puts them in danger

front: Name 2 causes of tire fires.
back: Low tire pressure and duals that touch

front: Truck is on fire. Should you pull into a gas station?
back: No, stop in an open area

front: Engine fire: should you open the hood?
back: No, not if you can avoid it
why: Spray through the grille or from underneath.

front: Cargo fire in a box trailer. Open the doors?
back: No, keep them shut
why: Air feeds the fire.

front: Where do you aim a fire extinguisher?
back: At the base of the fire

front: Where should you stand to fight a fire?
back: Upwind, as far back as you can

front: A B:C extinguisher works on what fires?
back: Electrical fires and burning liquids

front: Can you use water on an electric or gasoline fire?
back: No
why: Shock risk, and water spreads a gas fire.

front: Will coffee and fresh air sober you up?
back: No. Only time sobers you up
why: Not a cold shower, either.

front: Can cold medicine make you unsafe to drive?
back: Yes, it can make you drowsy

front: Where do hazmat papers go when you leave the cab?
back: On the driver's seat

front: How many placards must a placarded truck have?
back: At least 4 (front, rear, both sides)

front: Can you haul hazmat that needs no placards without an H endorsement?
back: Yes

front: You didn't load the cargo. Who must inspect it?
back: You, the driver

front: Besides miles and hours, when else do you recheck cargo?
back: After every break

front: What is GVWR?
back: Maker's max loaded weight for one vehicle

front: What does a bridge formula do?
back: Lowers weight for axles close together
why: It protects bridges and roads.

front: When might max legal weight be unsafe?
back: In bad weather or in mountains

front: High center of gravity makes what more likely?
back: Tipping over

front: How should you stack heavy and light cargo?
back: Heavy on the bottom, light on top

front: Too little weight on the front axle causes what?
back: Steering becomes unsafe

front: What is blocking?
back: Pieces fit snug against cargo to stop sliding

front: What is bracing?
back: Supports from top of cargo to floor or walls

front: Tie-downs must hold at least how much of the cargo weight?
back: Half (1/2) of the cargo weight
why: Add up the working load limits.

front: How many tie-downs per length of cargo?
back: 1 for every 10 feet

front: Smallest number of tie-downs for any load?
What does a header board do?
back: Keeps cargo from sliding into the cab

front: 2 reasons to cover cargo?
back: Protect people from spills; protect cargo from weather

front: You can't inspect a sealed load. What do you check?
back: Gross weight and axle weight limits

front: First railroad crossing violation: CDL loss?
back: At least 60 days
why: 2nd in 3 years: 120 days. 3rd: 1 year.

front: What 3 times do you inspect your truck?
back: Before, during, and after the trip
why: After the trip, you may write a report.

front: What do you check during a trip?
back: Gauges, mirrors, tires, brakes, lights, cargo
why: Look, listen, smell, and feel for trouble.

front: Name 3 key steering parts.
back: Steering column, gear box, tie rods
why: Look for bent, loose, or missing parts.

front: Name 3 suspension problems.
back: Broken springs, cracked hangers, leaking shocks
why: The suspension holds up the truck and its load.

front: Rust around the lug nuts may mean what?
back: The nuts are loose
why: Check that they are tight.

front: Is a wheel or rim with weld repairs safe?
back: No

front: Why is a leaking exhaust dangerous?
back: Poison fumes can get into the cab

front: Walk-around: name 3 things to check at the front.
back: Front axle, steering parts, windshield and wipers
why: Also lights and reflectors. Amber is the front color.

front: Why keep the key with you during inspection?
back: So no one can start or move the truck

front: What do you check wheel bearing seals for?
back: Leaks

front: Stopped on a hill: how do you start without rolling back?
back: Hold the parking brake until the engine pulls
why: Manual: let the clutch out a bit before leaving the brake.

front: Why use a helper when you back up?
back: You have blind spots you can't see

front: What are the 2 ways to know when to shift?
back: Engine speed (rpm) or road speed (mph)

front: Name the 2 special times to downshift.
back: Before a downhill and before a curve
why: In a curve, a little power keeps the truck steady.

front: When should you downshift an automatic?
back: Before you go down a grade
why: A low range gives more engine braking.

front: Do retarders keep you from skidding on slick roads?
back: No. They can make the drive wheels skid
why: Turn them off on wet, icy, or snowy roads.

front: What 2 main things do you look for ahead?
back: Traffic and road conditions
why: Look 12 to 15 seconds ahead.

front: Main way to see the sides and rear?
back: Your mirrors
why: Check them often and before every lane change.

front: What does "communicating" mean in safe driving?
back: Letting others know you're there and what you'll do
why: Signal early, flash brake lights, use the horn if needed.

front: Should you wave other drivers to pass you?
back: No. You could cause a crash
why: You could be blamed for it.

front: What is hydroplaning?
back: Tires ride on water and lose grip
why: It can start at 30 mph.

front: In heavy traffic, what is the safest speed?
back: The speed of the traffic around you
why: As long as it is legal and safe.

front: 30-foot truck at 55 mph: following distance?
back: 4 seconds
why: 3 seconds for 30 feet, plus 1 over 40 mph.

front: 60-foot rig under 40 mph: following distance?
back: 6 seconds
why: 1 second for every 10 feet.

front: 60-foot rig over 40 mph: following distance?
back: 7 seconds
why: Add 1 second over 40 mph.

front: How do you count your following distance?
back: Count seconds until you reach the spot it passed
why: Pick a mark the car ahead passes. Say "one thousand and one."

front: Where can a heavy truck get hung up underneath?
back: Dirt roads, dips, and rail tracks
why: A heavy load leaves little space below.

front: What is a hazard?
back: Any road condition or road user that may be dangerous

front: Why make a plan when you see a hazard?
back: So you're ready if it turns into an emergency

front: Why are delivery trucks a hazard?
back: Drivers hurry, hop out, or pull out fast
why: Packages and doors also block their view.

front: Name signs of a drunk or sleepy driver.
back: Weaving, drifting, stopping at green lights
why: An open window in cold weather is a clue too.

front: Texting or hand-held phone, 2nd offense in 3 years: penalty?
back: Lose CDL 60 days
why: 3rd offense: 120 days. Fines up to $2,750.

front: Is a hands-free phone free of distraction?
back: No. It distracts you, too
why: Hands-free distracts about as much as hand-held.

front: Name 3 ways to avoid distracted driving.
back: Phone off, set controls and route before you go

front: How can you spot a distracted driver?
back: Drifting, changing speed, busy with phone or food
why: Give them lots of room.

front: Aggressive driving vs. road rage: what is the difference?
back: Aggressive is pushy. Road rage tries to hurt someone

front: Name 3 ways to lower stress while driving.
back: Expect delays, relax, give others the benefit of the doubt

front: Should you use low beams whenever you can?
back: No. Use high beams when safe and legal
why: Dim them within 500 feet of other cars.

front: What can wet brakes do?
back: Get weak, pull to one side, or grab
why: Dry them with light brake pressure in low gear.

front: What sets your safe speed on a long downgrade?
back: Weight, grade length and steepness, road, weather

front: Why pick a low gear before going downhill?
back: You can't downshift once speed builds
why: You could lose all engine braking.

front: Downhill: which gear compared to going up the hill?
back: Often a lower gear than going up
why: New trucks roll easier, so the engine holds back less.

front: Downhill braking: how long does each brake press last?
back: About 3 seconds
why: Brake to 5 mph under safe speed, then let go.

front: What is an escape ramp?
back: A long bed of soft, loose material to stop runaways
why: Know where they are on your route.

front: Is stopping always the safest move in an emergency?
back: No. Steering around may be safer
why: You can turn faster than you can stop.

front: Path blocked: why is going right often best?
back: The shoulder is often empty. No head-on crash
why: Someone may be passing you on the left.

front: How do you know a truck has ABS?
back: A yellow ABS lamp on the dash
why: Trailers have a yellow lamp on the left side.

front: How do you protect a crash scene?
back: Move off the road, flashers on, set triangles
why: If you stop to help, park away from the crash.

front: A B:C extinguisher is not made for which fires?
back: Wood, paper, and cloth
why: Use an A:B:C extinguisher or water on those.

front: Name some causes of truck fires.
back: Crashes, bad tires, electric shorts, fuel, cargo
why: Low tires and duals that touch can catch fire.

front: What is a hazmat placard?
back: A diamond sign that shows the hazard class
why: It goes on the front, rear, and both sides.

front: Why are placards used?
back: To warn others of hazardous cargo
why: Rescuers need to know what you are hauling.

front: Where do hazmat papers go while you drive?
back: In a door pouch, or in view and in reach
why: On the seat when you leave the cab.

front: What is a hazmat ID number?
back: A 4-digit code after UN or NA
why: The ERG book tells what each number means.

front: When do you need a tank endorsement?
back: Tanks over 119 gallons each, 1,000+ gallons total
why: The liquid does not have to be hazmat.

front: Name the driver's 4 cargo duties.
back: Inspect, spot overloads, secure it, keep view and gear clear
why: This is your job even if someone else loaded it.

front: GCWR vs. GCW: what is the difference?
back: GCWR is the max rating. GCW is the real weight
why: GCW is the tractor, trailers, and cargo together.

front: Fewest tie-downs for a 20-foot load?
why: 1 per 10 feet: 20 feet needs 2.
